messages.author: 995acdc01429b8fa
messages.subject: Why there are no _pdf functions?
parts:
I see in manual that there are only _lpdf functions, like normal_lpdf, student_t_lpdf etc.. Why don't we have _pdf functions too?

I need pdf in some of my calculations, so every time I have to expontiate lpdf or I would have to write my custom pdf function, even for the most common distributions.

Also, it would be nice to have a Variance-Gamma distribution
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance-gamma_distribution
It should be straightforward to implement since all special functions that are used for it are available in Stan.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why there are no _pdf functions?
parts:
Hi Denis,

We compute everything on the log scale for numeric stability.

The reason why we don't add things to the language for convenience is really a practical one. It's a maintenance burden. Rather than having the Stan language support another 30+ functions, you can easily write exp(foo_lpdf(...)) and be done with it. If Stan exposed it, then it's on Stan to indicate when it underflows to 0 or overflows to 1 and we'd have a ton more work to do. If it were free to do it, we would just implement it.

On Wed, Dec 7, 2016 at 12:07 PM, Denis Perevalov <deni...@gmail.com> wrote:
I see in manual that there are only _lpdf functions, like normal_lpdf, student_t_lpdf etc.. Why don't we have _pdf functions too?

I need pdf in some of my calculations, so every time I have to expontiate lpdf or I would have to write my custom pdf function, even for the most common distributions.
Yes, just do that. Althought... you're probably writing your function wrong. Just computing things on the log scale.

Also, it would be nice to have a Variance-Gamma distribution
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance-gamma_distribution
It should be straightforward to implement since all special functions that are used for it are available in Stan.

Great! Go ahead and write a custom lpdf function in your program. I think that absolute value in there might introduce a discontinuity, so it might not be something that should go in Stan in general. And I forget if the modified Bessel function of the second kind is exposed in the Stan language. If it's not, it's probably because we can't get reasonable gradients out of it. For Stan's algorithms, gradients are required, so it's more than just being able to compute the log joint probability distribution function. You need to be able to compute the gradients also.


Good luck with the Variance-Gamma distribution! Let us know you're able to get a working version with a function.


Daniel

messages.author: 995acdc01429b8fa
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why there are no _pdf functions?
parts:
Hi Bob,

An example of the problem where I want _pdf is as follows.

Suppose I have a time series of daily returns. I have a model that predicts a distribution of returns. So each sample(simulation) predicts its own probability of returns - not a number but a distribution. Usually I use a normal pdf. So, for every day I have lots of return pdfs after I train my Bayesian model on a training sample. Now I want to compute a metric of how my model performed on a testing sample. Each day I observe only single return. Overall lpdf for every j-th day will be 

lpdf_j = log(1/N * sum_i=1^N  pdf_i(r_j)), where the sum is over simulations.

So, I would need to average the pdfs, not lpdfs, and then take a log. The way I do it right now, I compute vector of pdf_i in the generated quantities and then get it with get_posterior_mean in PyStan interface. That takes care of the averaging.

I could record all lpdfs or pdfs for each sample and each day. But then I'd have to make the above computation offline. And in Python it can take a long time. Also, this kind of run would require to store it in memory. But if I exclude lpdf vector that I compute in generated from parameters that I pass to pystan.stan, then it's not stored in memory, but the mean is still stored in memory and could be obtained with get_posterior_mean function on the StanFit object. This was previously discussed here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Average$20over$20simulations%7Csort:relevance/stan-users/GbZ4_1mR98k/aiBwjI6mBwAJ



With regard to Variance-Gamma. I can implement it in the Stan language, no problem. If it works fine and needs to be committed to Stan repository does it need to be in a C++ implementation?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Why there are no _pdf functions?
parts:
> On Dec 7, 2016, at 3:41 PM, Denis Perevalov <deni...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> An example of the problem where I want _pdf is as follows.
>
> Suppose I have a time series of daily returns. I have a model that predicts a distribution of returns. So each sample(simulation) predicts its own probability of returns - not a number but a distribution. Usually I use a normal pdf. So, for every day I have lots of return pdfs after I train my Bayesian model on a training sample. Now I want to compute a metric of how my model performed on a testing sample. Each day I observe only single return. Overall lpdf for every j-th day will be
>
> lpdf_j = log(1/N * sum_i=1^N pdf_i(r_j)), where the sum is over simulations.

Great. That's easy. You can program that much much more stably
as:

vector[N] lp;
for (n in 1:N) lp[n] = foo_lpdf( ...n... );
lpdf_j = log_sum_exp(lp) - log(N);

where you just assign the lpdf term to lp. log_sum_exp does
sums on the linear scale of inputs on the log scale and
returns a result on the log scale, all while maintaining maximal
arithmetic precision (not to mention avoiding underflow and overflow).
> With regard to Variance-Gamma. I can implement it in the Stan language, no problem. If it works fine and needs to be committed to Stan repository does it need to be in a C++ implementation?

Implementing a distribution for Stan itself is much more work
because we want them to be vectorized (template expressions)
compute return types (template metaprogram) and drop constant terms
(template traits). And we need it not just for reverse-mode autodiff
but also for forward mode (requiring additional template expressions).
And we require extenstive testing using our density testing framework.
You can see how that goes for existing distributions in the code.
It's in the stan-dev/math repo.

- Bob
